ruling: Ordering runs in three stages: within 6-8 weeks the proximate-cause entity (developer or operator, whichever attribution names) announces a visible process/governance change while its model line keeps shipping unchanged; within the following 30-60 days formal state action (a licensing invocation against the operator, or liability language on an already-moving bill) lands, arriving after and distinct from the voluntary move; only after that formal action names the other party does it make an equivalent move, 8-16 weeks out and conditional, with symmetric or absent movement on both sides falsifying the whole sequence.
because: pressure-model's round-2 revision is the only minute that actually stages the question asked: it orders the proximate-cause entity's move ahead of the other party's, makes the second move conditional on and lagged behind the first, and gives an explicit falsifier (symmetric or null action). ai-public-backlash's round-2 revision supplies the second joint: voluntary lab/operator concession precedes formal state or regulatory action rather than following it. lab-moves supplies the third fact needed to complete the chain — the process-change announcement coexists with continued shipping, meaning the move is governance-layer, not capability-layer.
threat_live: Governance-layer announcements (a safety framework, an audit commitment, a review gate) become available as a substitute for capability-layer restraint — the model line keeps shipping — which is newly dangerous because it lets 'compliance visible cost' satisfy the political/legal pressure that ai-pressure and lab-moves describe without the underlying capability ever being curtailed; separately, per ai-regulation-teeth, rules with only disclosure power get cited as if they were the response but carry no enforcement, so the appearance of a regulatory stage can arrive without the stage's substance.
strongest_minute: pressure-model (v2.1, round 2) — it is the only minute that revised specifically to add sequencing (who moves first, how long the other party's move can lag, and under what condition) rather than just re-asserting a flat trigger window, and it names the exact falsification condition (symmetric or neither-moves) that a dated check can apply.
weakest_minute: ai-incident-severity — its round-2 DEFEND doubles down on 'rapid convergence onto joint liability standards' but supplies no dated, checkable observable for that convergence, which the question explicitly requires; declining to classify systemic-vs-one-off is honest, but the positive claim it does make is unfalsifiable as stated.
shared_assumption: That settled, quantified, public attribution mechanically produces a public, dated institutional response rather than quiet settlement, sealed litigation, or delayed non-public action — assumed by five of six minutes and engaged as an objection by only one (ai-pressure round 2, citing standard counsel advice to minimize public statements under live liability exposure).
smuggled_assumption: ai-regulation-teeth smuggles in that licensing/audit power attaches to the operator rather than the developer — a claim it flags itself in round 2 as 'bolted onto the mechanism, not derived from it' — and the brief grants only that attribution settles, not onto which of the two entities enforcement power specifically lands.
unresolved: Which entity is the proximate-cause first-mover — developer (ai-pressure, lab-moves), operator (ai-regulation-teeth), or both jointly (ai-incident-severity) — is not settled by the brief and the minutes argue past each other on it rather than resolving it; the staged sequence above is conditional on whichever entity attribution actually names, which the minutes cannot supply from a single incident.
